responses.final.system_synthesis:
Robotics software is hard because there's so much to account for at once, before the robot even moves. There are sensors that can give bad or missing data, timing issues where things don't happen in the expected order, physical factors like speed and how the robot actually reacts to commands, and safety concerns where a bug doesn't just throw an error, it can make the robot crash into something for real. So hardware, software, timing, and safety all have to be considered together.
The architecture implemented here decides move or stop based on lidar readings in front of the robot. Pro: simple and easy to reason about, just check distance and decide. Con: it misses a lot, like ground slipperiness, or whether the robot's current speed means it needs more room to stop, or whether turning instead of full-stopping would be smarter.
For the ROS 2 middleware, there were at least four components talking to each other. The lidar publishes scan data, the control node reads that and decides a proposed speed, that proposed velocity goes out on /student_cmd_vel, the command guard node subscribes to that topic and checks it, then republishes an approved velocity on /cmd_vel which the robot/simulator actually executes. Lidar-to-control-node, control-node-to-guard, and guard-to-robot, three links connecting four pieces.
Timing and invalid data matter a lot here because if a reading is missing, late, or wrong and the code doesn't handle it properly, the robot could keep moving with no real idea what's in front of it. That's why missing data gets treated as "stop" instead of "assume clear," since assuming clear could cause a crash.
The layer that can actually restrict unsafe motion is the command guard, since it sits between the proposed command and the real robot and can block or override anything unsafe before it reaches the motors.

responses.mission_2.safety_explanation: The command guard checks the proposed command given to the robot and alters or rejects the command if they are not safe. The final zero command stops all movement when a trial ends so that no sudden unexpected movements are executed after the trial. The stale-command timeout is needed if the robot is no longer receiving communication from a node that could be vital in keeping the robot in a functioning state.
responses.mission_3.data_to_command:
The first function 'front_distance' finds the distance of the closest obstacle in front of it from the LiDAR. It does so by putting the values from the LiDAR into a list, finds the angle using the angle_increment of each value and angle_min. Using the angle, we determine whether the value is in front of the robot and is a valid value. Out of the distances we have left, we get the closest one to our robot.

 Then the second function 'decide_velocity' and it stops the robot if there is no given distance or if the distance to travel is shorter than equal to the determined distance from an object in front of it. Otherwise, if neither of those are flagged, we tell the robot to move.
responses.mission_3.missing_data_safety: The robot stops when there is not valid front measurement because it means we don't know if the path in front of it is clear. It could be a that our LiDAR sensor bugged out or something else unexpected happened. But to treat the path as clear and have the robot to continue forward is risky.
responses.mission_3.system_layers: The decision functions and the supplied ROS node, as well as the command guard work together to help move the robot. First, the LiDAR values are passed through the functions and fed into the command guards. The command guard checks to make sure the values are safe to pass through and the ROS node receives the value from the command guard to move the actual part.
